title: Polite Requests in Spanish: How to Ask for Things Nicely

meta_description: Polite requests in Spanish: ¿puedes…?, ¿podría…?, ¿te importaría…?, quería, ¿me pones…?, softeners and when a direct request is perfectly polite.

body_html:
Polite requests in Spanish work on a scale, from the friendly ¿Me pasas la sal? to the very formal ¿Sería tan amable de…?. Learners often worry that Spanish requests sound too direct, and they sometimes are, but often they’re perfectly polite. What makes a request polite in Spanish is the verb form, a few softening words and your tone. Here’s how to ask for anything, in any situation, without sounding rude or robotic.

Key takeaways
  • Friendly: ¿Me pasas…?, ¿Puedes…?
  • Polite: ¿Podría…?, Quería…, ¿Me podría…?
  • Very polite: ¿Le importaría…?, ¿Sería tan amable de…?
  • In shops and bars, short direct requests are normal: Un café, por favor.
{{toc}}

Polite requests in Spanish: the politeness scale

LevelSpanishEnglish
Friendly¿Me pasas el agua?Pass me the water?
Neutral¿Puedes ayudarme?Can you help me?
Polite¿Podrías ayudarme?Could you help me?
Polite (formal)¿Me podría decir la hora?Could you tell me the time?
Very polite¿Le importaría cerrar la ventana?Would you mind closing the window?
Extremely formal¿Sería tan amable de esperar un momento?Would you be so kind as to wait a moment?

The conditional (podría, importaría, sería) softens a request just like “could” and “would” in English. The RAE’s Nueva gramática describes this “courtesy conditional”.

The present tense: friendly and natural

Among friends and family, a present-tense question is the normal way to ask: ¿Me pasas el pan? (Will you pass me the bread?), ¿Me ayudas con esto? (Will you help me with this?), ¿Me dejas tu cargador? (Will you lend me your charger?). It’s warm, not rude. Using ¿Podrías…? with your best friend for something tiny can even sound oddly distant.

Quería: the soft “I’d like”

In shops, offices and on the phone, the imperfect quería is a very common soft request: Quería un kilo de tomates (I’d like a kilo of tomatoes), Quería pedir cita (I’d like to make an appointment). Quisiera is even more formal. Plain quiero can sound demanding in some contexts, though with por favor and a smile it’s usually fine.

{{image:2}}

Softening words

  • por favor please
  • si no es mucha molestia if it’s not too much trouble
  • cuando puedas when you can
  • un momentito / un favorcito diminutives make requests gentler
  • perdona que te moleste sorry to bother you
  • ¿Te importa si…? Do you mind if…?

Example: Perdona que te moleste, ¿me podrías hacer un favorcito cuando puedas?

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Requests in shops, bars and restaurants

Service situations use short, direct requests. In Mexico: ¿Me da un taco de pastor? In Colombia: ¿Me regala un tinto? And if you travel to Spain, bars are even more direct: ¿Me pones una caña? or Ponme un café sounds friendly there, not rude. (literally “will you gift me a coffee?”, but you pay!). These are all normal and polite. See {{link:ordering-food-in-spanish|ordering food in Spanish}}.

Asking for permission

  • ¿Puedo pasar? May I come in?
  • ¿Te importa si abro la ventana? Do you mind if I open the window?
  • ¿Se puede? May I? (when knocking or entering)
  • ¿Le molesta que me siente aquí? Do you mind if I sit here?

Note the subjunctive after ¿Le molesta que…?. For “can” vs “know how to”, see {{link:poder-vs-saber|poder vs saber}}.

Requests at work and in emails

Professional requests combine the conditional with a brief reason and a thank-you: ¿Podrías enviarme el informe antes del viernes? Lo necesito para la reunión. ¡Gracias! In emails, Le agradecería que… + subjunctive is a classic: Le agradecería que me confirmara la fecha (I would be grateful if you could confirm the date). See {{link:writing-emails-in-spanish|writing emails in Spanish}} and {{link:talking-to-coworkers-in-spanish|talking to coworkers in Spanish}}.

A sample conversation

  • A: Perdone, ¿le importaría bajar un poco la música? (Excuse me, would you mind turning the music down a bit?)
  • B: Ay, perdón, claro que no. (Oh, sorry, of course not.)
  • A: Muchas gracias, muy amable. (Thank you very much, that’s very kind.)

Saying thank you and responding

A request isn’t finished until you thank the person. Beyond gracias, try muchas gracias, muy amable (very kind), te lo agradezco (I appreciate it) or, among friends, ¡eres un sol! (you’re a star!). When someone asks you for something, answer warmly: ¡Claro!, Por supuesto, Sin problema or Con mucho gusto. If you have to say no, soften it: Lo siento, ahora mismo no puedo, ¿te va bien más tarde?, which keeps the relationship friendly.

Regional notes

Politeness norms vary. In Spain, short direct requests are normal and people say por favor less than learners. In Mexico and Colombia, requests tend to be softer and more indirect, with diminutives (un cafecito, ahorita) and usted used more often. When in doubt, mirror the people around you.

Remember too that tone of voice does a lot of the work: a warm, rising intonation turns even a short ¿Me ayudas? into a friendly request rather than a demand.

Common mistakes

MistakeBetterWhy
¿Puedo tener un café?¿Me da un café?Literal translation
¿Le importaría que abro?¿Le importaría que abriera?Subjunctive needed
Dame eso. (to a stranger)¿Me da eso, por favor?Too abrupt
¿Podría usted por favor amablemente…?¿Podría…, por favor?Over-softened
{{image:3}}

Final thoughts

Match the form to the situation: present tense for friends, quería and ¿me da? in shops, conditionals for strangers and formal settings. Add a softener and a warm gracias, and every request will land well. For more everyday situations, see {{link:spanish-phrases-for-everyday-situations|my guide to Spanish phrases for everyday situations}}.

faq.q: How do you make a polite request in Spanish?
faq.a: Use the conditional: ¿Podría ayudarme?, ¿Le importaría…? You can also use quería (I’d like) in shops and offices.

faq.q: Is it rude to say quiero in Spanish?
faq.a: Not necessarily, but quería or ¿me pone…? sounds softer, especially in shops and restaurants.

faq.q: How do you say “would you mind…?” in Spanish?
faq.a: ¿Te importaría…? (informal) or ¿Le importaría…? (formal), followed by an infinitive: ¿Le importaría esperar?
